pharm: Dibenzothiazepine; antagonist at dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors (active metabolite norquetiapine adds norepinephrine transporter inhibition)
quick: Schizophrenia IR: target 150-750 mg/day (max 750); bipolar depression: 300 mg/day at bedtime
IR: with or without food; XR: without food or with a light meal (<300 kcal)
Use only if needed; 3rd-trimester EPS/withdrawal risk in neonate
Low relative infant dose (<1%); use with caution, monitor infant for sedation
Start IR 25 mg/day; titrate slowly, higher levels expected
Weight/BMI, fasting glucose, lipids, BP (esp. children/adolescents)
summary: Quetiapine is an atypical antipsychotic available in immediate-release (IR) and extended-release (XR) forms for schizophrenia, bipolar mania, bipolar depression, bipolar I maintenance (as adjunct to lithium or divalproex), and—XR only—as adjunct for major depressive disorder. It is highly sedating and commonly causes weight gain, hyperglycemia, and dyslipidemia, requiring routine metabolic monitoring. It carries boxed warnings for increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis and for increased suicidality in children, adolescents, and young adults.
indications: Bipolar I disorder, acute manic episodes (adults as monotherapy or adjunct to lithium/divalproex; children/adolescents 10-17 years as monotherapy)
Bipolar disorder, depressive episodes (adults; bipolar I and II)
Bipolar I disorder maintenance, as adjunct to lithium or divalproex (adults)
Adjunctive treatment of major depressive disorder (extended-release XR only, adults)

Start 50 mg/day; increase in 50 mg/day increments per response

admin: Immediate-release tablets may be taken with or without food
Extended-release (XR) tablets: swallow whole, do not split, chew, or crush; take without food or with a light meal (<300 kcal), generally in the evening
Bipolar depression: dose once daily at bedtime regardless of formulation
Obtain baseline weight, fasting glucose, lipids, and blood pressure before starting
Reduce dose to one-sixth with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors; increase up to 5-fold with potent CYP3A4 inducers
If restarting after >1 week off therapy, follow the initial titration schedule again
moa: Mechanism in these indications is not fully established but is believed to involve combined antagonism of dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2 (5-HT2A) receptors. The active metabolite norquetiapine has similar D2 but greater 5-HT2A activity and inhibits the norepinephrine transporter, which may contribute to antidepressant effect. Antagonism at histamine H1 (sedation, weight gain), alpha-1 adrenergic (orthostatic hypotension), and muscarinic receptors (anticholinergic effects) accounts for much of the tolerability profile.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to quetiapine or any formulation component (anaphylaxis reported)
relative: Elderly with dementia-related psychosis (boxed warning - increased mortality and cerebrovascular events)
Children/young adults with depression (boxed warning - suicidality)
Cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease, conditions predisposing to hypotension
QT prolongation risk or concomitant QT-prolonging drugs
History of seizures or low seizure threshold
Pre-existing low WBC / history of drug-induced leukopenia
monitor: Suicidal thoughts/behavior, especially early and at dose changes
Lens/cataract exam at baseline and every 6 months in chronic use

preg: Use only if clearly needed. Neonates exposed in the third trimester are at risk for extrapyramidal and/or withdrawal symptoms (agitation, hypertonia, hypotonia, tremor, somnolence, respiratory distress, feeding difficulty), varying in severity; monitor and manage accordingly. Published data have not established a drug-associated risk of major birth defects or miscarriage. Untreated maternal illness carries its own risks. Enroll patients in the National Pregnancy Registry for Atypical Antipsychotics (1-866-961-2388).
lact: Quetiapine is present in human milk at a relative infant dose of less than 1% of the maternal weight-adjusted dosage, with no consistent adverse events reported in breastfed infants. Effect on milk production is unknown. Weigh the benefits of breastfeeding against the mother's clinical need and any potential effects on the infant; monitor the breastfed infant for somnolence and poor feeding.
renal: No dosage adjustment required. Severe renal impairment (CrCl 10-30 mL/min) lowers mean oral clearance by about 25%, but plasma concentrations remain within the normal range; quetiapine is highly metabolized and minimally renally excreted.
hepatic: Quetiapine is extensively hepatically metabolized, so higher plasma levels are expected in hepatic impairment (mean clearance ~30% lower; some patients show 3-fold higher AUC/Cmax). Start at 25 mg/day and increase in 25-50 mg/day increments to an effective dose with close monitoring. Transient, reversible transaminase elevations are common early in therapy.

major: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors - ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir, indinavir, nefazodone (markedly raise levels; reduce quetiapine to one-sixth dose)
Potent CYP3A4 inducers - phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampin, St. John's wort (lower levels ~5-fold; increase quetiapine up to 5-fold)
QT-prolonging drugs - Class IA/III antiarrhythmics, other antipsychotics, certain antibiotics (avoid combination)
CNS depressants / alcohol (additive sedation and impairment)
moderate: Anticholinergic drugs (additive antimuscarinic effects, risk of ileus/obstruction)
Levodopa and dopamine agonists (antagonized by quetiapine)
Drugs causing electrolyte imbalance (hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia increase QT/torsades risk)
interactions.food: IR: food has minimal effect (Cmax +25%, AUC +15%). XR: high-fat meals increase exposure, so take without food or with a light meal (<300 kcal)
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; quetiapine potentiated alcohol's cognitive and motor effects in trials
interactions.diagnostics: May elevate fasting glucose, lipids, prolactin, and transaminases; lowers thyroid hormones (T4) and may raise TSH. Can cause false-positive urine immunoassays for methadone and tricyclic antidepressants

serious: Hyperglycemia / new-onset or worsening diabetes, ketoacidosis
emergency: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability)

monitoring: Weight and BMI at baseline, weeks 4, 8, and 12, then quarterly
Fasting glucose / HbA1c at baseline, ~12 weeks, then annually
Fasting lipid panel at baseline and periodically
Blood pressure and orthostatic symptoms; BP also at baseline and periodically in children/adolescents
Extrapyramidal symptoms, akathisia, and tardive dyskinesia
Suicidality, mood, and behavioral changes, especially early and at dose changes
CBC during the first months if pre-existing low WBC or prior drug-induced neutropenia
TSH and free T4 at baseline and follow-up; prolactin if symptomatic
Lens/cataract examination at initiation and at 6-month intervals during chronic therapy
counsel: Expect possible weight gain and drowsiness; follow diet, exercise, and metabolic monitoring
Report excessive thirst, urination, hunger, or weakness (high blood sugar)
Rise slowly to avoid dizziness and falls, especially during titration
Use caution with driving or hazardous machinery until effects are known; avoid alcohol
Swallow XR tablets whole and take without a heavy meal; do not crush or chew
Watch for new or worsening depression, agitation, or suicidal thoughts and report immediately
Report fever, sore throat, or infection (possible low white cell count) and muscle stiffness with high fever (NMS)
Do not stop abruptly; taper to avoid withdrawal symptoms. Tell clinician about pregnancy, breastfeeding, and all medications
pk: Sedation within hours; antipsychotic/mood effect over days to weeks
IR usually BID; XR and bipolar-depression dosing once daily
20-25 C (68-77 F); excursions permitted 15-30 C (59-86 F)
pearls: Highly sedating and anticholinergic; low doses are widely misused off-label for insomnia despite metabolic and other risks
Boxed warnings: increased mortality in elderly dementia psychosis and increased suicidality in children, adolescents, and young adults
Strong CYP3A4 substrate - cut dose to one-sixth with strong inhibitors and raise up to 5-fold with potent inducers
Extended-release (XR) is the only form FDA-approved as adjunct for major depressive disorder; bipolar depression is dosed once daily at bedtime
Avoid combinations with QT-prolonging drugs and correct hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia before use
Causes dose-related decreases in thyroid hormone (T4); check TSH and free T4 at baseline and follow-up
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip it; do not double up. For once-daily bedtime or XR regimens, resume the normal schedule. After more than one week off therapy, contact the prescriber, as the initial titration may need to be repeated.
overdose: Signs reflect exaggerated pharmacology: drowsiness, sedation, tachycardia, hypotension, anticholinergic toxicity, and in severe cases coma, delirium, QT prolongation, and (rarely) death. Establish and maintain an airway with adequate oxygenation/ventilation; begin continuous cardiac/ECG monitoring for arrhythmias. Treatment is supportive (IV fluids and pressors for hypotension, avoiding agents that may worsen it); there is no specific antidote. Patients with pre-existing severe cardiovascular disease are at higher risk. Contact a Regional Poison Control Center (1-800-222-1222).
